Every line comes from a logger named after the part of ropt that produced it, and all of them sit under ropt, which is why setting the level there covers the library. Setting it on one of the names below covers that part alone, which is the quickest way to follow a single mechanism: put ropt.components.executors at DEBUG to watch jobs being submitted without the per-batch traffic.

Logger Emits ropt.components.compute_steps the start and finish of an optimization or evaluation, and the configuration it started from ropt.core per-batch realization counts, stopping conditions, optimizer callbacks, and reuse of cached results ropt.components.executors executor start-up, job submission and cancellation, retained working directories, and exceptions raised by work that an aborted call no longer waits for ropt.components.evaluators work-item dispatch ropt.components.event_handlers each new best objective, and any handler that raised ropt.backend.scipy, ropt.backend.external the method in use, and the external subprocess lifecycle ropt.plugins plugin registration

DEBUG traces the mechanism: one line per optimizer callback, per dispatched batch and per cluster job, plus the configuration the optimization started from. It is verbose — a gradient-based method requests functions and gradients separately on most iterations, and each request is a line — but it is what to attach to a bug report.

docs.title: Running Multiple Optimizations
docs.text:
Several optimizations can run together rather than one after another. Wrap each optimize call in a zero-argument callable and pass the callables to run with a thread pool. run starts each one on a worker of that pool and returns the results in the order the callables were given:

from functools import partial

from ropt import optimize, run, session

with session() as s:
    pool = s.thread_pool(workers=4)
    runner = s.thread_pool(workers=len(start_points))
    results = run(
        [partial(optimize, config, x0, objective, pool=pool) for x0 in start_points],
        pool=runner,
    )

Each callable is an ordinary optimize call, so every optimization can have its own configuration, initial values, objective, metadata and report callback.

The optimizations need a pool of their own, runner here, separate from the pool they evaluate on. A call made from work running on a pool cannot use that same pool: it raises WorkflowError. Without a pool, run calls the functions one after another on the calling thread.

Give each optimization an ID

Pass metadata to tag each optimization with an identifier that is attached to its results (and shows up in a DataFrameHandler's tables):

labels = ["low", "mid", "high"]
results = run(
    [
        partial(
            optimize, config, x0, objective, pool=pool, metadata={"label": label}
        )
        for x0, label in zip(start_points, labels)
    ],
    pool=runner,
)
for result in results:
    print(result.results.metadata["label"])

See Attaching metadata for details.

docs.title: Two levels of concurrency
docs.text:
There are two independent levels of concurrency here:

  • The optimizations run concurrently, each on a worker of the pool given to run. The number of workers of that pool caps how many of them are under way at the same time; the others wait for a free worker.
  • The function evaluations inside those optimizations happen on the pool passed to each optimize call, and the pool determines how they are parallelized. With thread_pool(workers=1) the optimizations still progress together, but their evaluations are executed one at a time. A larger pool — thread_pool(workers=n), or a process or HPC pool — runs several evaluations at once.

One pool is one budget: workers=10 means ten evaluations at a time across all the optimizations that use the pool, not ten per optimization. Batch IDs stay distinct whatever you pass, since every optimization in the program draws them from one counter.

examples/multiple_optimizations.py runs one optimization per start vector, at most two at a time, and tags each with its own metadata:

with session() as s:
    job = partial(optimize, CONFIG, pool=s.thread_pool(workers=3))
    results = run(
        [
            partial(job, start, rosenbrock, metadata={"label": label})
            for label, start in enumerate(STARTS)
        ],
        pool=s.thread_pool(workers=2),
    )

docs.title: Watching optimizations that overlap
docs.text:
report= belongs to one optimize call: give each optimization its own callback, or the same one to all of them. handlers= takes handlers that several optimizations may feed together — see Sharing a handler across concurrent optimizations.

A shared report= callback is called by every optimization at once

Each optimization calls its callback on its own thread. Nothing serializes those calls, so a callback that appends to a list, updates a counter, or writes a file needs a lock of its own. Give each optimization its own callback when they must stay apart, or pass a handler in handlers=, which takes a lock around every event it handles.

A shared handler makes the optimizations wait for each other

That lock is not free. An optimization that emits a result waits until the handler has finished with it, and a second optimization waits for the first. A slow handler therefore throttles all of them, once per result produced.

So keep a shared handler cheap. A handler that must do slow work — writing a file, talking to a database — holds up every optimization feeding it.

Without a pool, the workers of run do the evaluating

An optimization started with optimize without a pool evaluates in your own program, on the worker of run that runs it. When several of them run at once, your evaluation function is called by several threads at once and must tolerate that. Start them on a pool when it must not be.

Not every backend can take part

An optimizer that needs a working directory of its own, writes to a file whose name is fixed, or keeps state inside its library between calls cannot run while anything else is running in the same process — another optimization of its own kind included. Each backend documents whether this applies to it. Select it as external/... and it gets a process of its own, where none of that is shared.

Optimizer output capture is likewise for one optimization at a time. If more than one of them sets stdout or stderr, the second to start raises WorkflowError. Leave both unset here, and set verbose=False unless you want the optimizers' reports interleaved on the terminal.

docs.title: Failure in one optimization
docs.text:
The optimizations started from the callables of one run call are nested in it. When one of them raises, run aborts the others and raises that exception at once. Failures and Aborts gives the rules for every case. An aborted optimization raises AbortedError with ABORTED_ON_ERROR — at once on a pool, or at its next evaluation boundary without one — but run does not wait for it, and its result is lost. Optimizations still waiting for a worker are not started after the abort.

A callable that catches the exception of its optimization does not fail, so the other optimizations are not aborted. Catch the exceptions you expect, and return something that marks the failure:

def optimize_or_none(x0):
    try:
        return optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=pool)
    except SimulationError:
        return None

results = run([partial(optimize_or_none, x0) for x0 in start_points], pool=runner)

SimulationError stands for an exception that your own objective raises.

Session.abort reaches every optimization on the session's pools, and run then raises AbortedError with USER_ABORT. When a failure aborted it, the exit code is ABORTED_ON_ERROR, so the exit code distinguishes an abort that was asked for from one that a failure caused. A KeyboardInterrupt aborts the optimizations of the run call it passes through, and is raised at once. See Exit Codes for what each code means.

docs.title: Aborting from outside
docs.text:
The report callback runs inside the optimization it stops, which is no use to a signal handler or a user interface. Session.abort is the one that is called from another thread: it aborts every call given one of the session's pools or made in its with block, and each raises AbortedError with USER_ABORT.

with session() as s:
    pool = s.thread_pool(workers=4)
    signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, lambda *_: s.abort())
    try:
        result = optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=pool)
    except AbortedError as error:
        print("aborted:", error.exit_code.message)

The two are not the same kind of ending, which is why they have different exit codes. A report callback stops the optimization on a criterion, at a point it chose, and the optimization returns the best result it had reached. An abort applies no criterion, and the optimization returns no result. To keep what an aborted optimization had reached, collect its results as they arrive, with a report callback or a handler.

An aborted optimization does not wait for the evaluations that are running. With no pool, the optimization runs the evaluation function itself, so the evaluation in progress returns first. On a thread or process pool, the evaluations already running continue after the optimization has ended, and their workers are free only once they return. On an HPC pool they are cancelled.

An abort is permanent: the session stays aborted. A call given one of its pools afterwards, or in its with block, raises AbortedError with USER_ABORT at once. Code that catches the AbortedError inside the block can record what happened, but cannot start more work on the session; catching it outside the with block works as well. To try again, open a new session. A run call is aborted as a whole: a callable still waiting for a worker is not started. Leaving the session's with block aborts its calls as well, and then releases its pools, which is what refuses a call made after that. Releasing an HPC pool cancels the jobs it still has, so none are left running when the block has ended. A call aborted that way raises with ABORTED rather than USER_ABORT, since it was the block ending rather than a request to abort.

A call without a pool, such as optimize, made in the with block of a session, is aborted with the session. Made outside any session block, it cannot be aborted this way.

docs.title: Nested Optimization
docs.text:
Some problems split naturally into two layers: a few variables that are awkward for one method — integers, say, or switches — and the rest, which a gradient method handles well. Nested optimization solves them in two loops. An outer optimization varies the awkward variables, and every outer evaluation runs a complete inner optimization over the remaining ones, returning the best value it reached.

This page also covers four things that are not nesting

Nesting itself is a niche, but this page puts four things that are not into one program small enough to read end to end: choosing a pool per layer, and why one of them has to stay on threads; collecting results from optimizations that overlap in time, in one handler; reusing an evaluation the optimizer has already made; and moving the expensive layer to a cluster by changing a single line.

Nothing in ropt is dedicated to this: the outer evaluation function calls optimize itself. What needs care is the plumbing around it — which variables each layer owns, which pool each layer evaluates on, and how to get the results out.

flowchart TB
    subgraph proc["your process"]
        direction LR
        outer["outer optimize<br/>(integer variables)"]
        subgraph touter["outer thread_pool — 2 threads"]
            direction TB
            in1["outer eval →<br/>inner optimize"]
            in2["outer eval →<br/>inner optimize"]
        end
        grp["shared<br/>DataFrameHandler"]
        outer --> in1
        outer --> in2
        in1 -.->|"results"| grp
        in2 -.->|"results"| grp
    end
    subgraph pinner["inner process_pool — 2 workers"]
        direction TB
        w1["worker"]
        w2["worker"]
    end
    in1 ==>|"batch"| w1
    in2 ==>|"batch"| w2

Solid arrows start an optimization, thick arrows carry evaluations out to a worker process, and dotted arrows carry results back to the handler. Both pools are drawn: the outer one is inside your process, the inner one is not. The sections below work through each part.

The runnable script for this page is examples/nested_optimization.py. It needs the polars extra.

docs.title: Splitting the variables
docs.text:
Both layers describe the same variable vector; each is handed the half it may change. The mask field does this, and the two masks are complements:

DIM = 4
REALIZATIONS = 5
MASK = [True, True, False, False]
INNER_CONFIG: dict[str, Any] = {
    "variables": {
        "variable_count": DIM,
        "perturbation_magnitudes": 1e-6,
        "mask": MASK,
        "lower_bounds": 0.0,
        "upper_bounds": 10.0,
    },
    "realizations": {"weights": [1.0] * REALIZATIONS},
    "optimizer": {"max_functions": 8},
}

OUTER_CONFIG: dict[str, Any] = {
    "variables": {
        "variable_count": DIM,
        "mask": np.logical_not(MASK),
        "lower_bounds": 0.0,
        "upper_bounds": 10.0,
        "types": "integer",
    },
    "realizations": {"weights": [1.0]},
    "backend": {
        "method": "differential_evolution",
        "options": {"rng": 4},
        "parallel": True,
        "max_iterations": 4,
    },
}

A masked-out variable keeps the value it was given and is not passed to the optimizer, so the inner optimization treats the outer variables as constants and the outer optimization never touches the inner ones. The two layers can otherwise be configured completely differently — here the outer is integer-valued and gradient-free, while the inner is continuous and uses an ensemble of five realizations. See variables for the field, and Discrete and Mixed-Integer Variables for the outer method.

docs.title: The outer evaluation function
docs.text:
An outer evaluation is an inner optimization. The function receives the outer variables, merges them into a full vector, runs optimize, and returns the best objective it found:

key = (context.realization, *variables.tolist())
if key in memo:
    return memo[key]

result = optimize(
    INNER_CONFIG,
    np.where(MASK, INITIAL_VALUES, variables),
    function,
    pool=pool,
    handlers=[tables],
    # Within a batch only (batch_id, row_idx) is unique: several rows share
    # a realization, so realization alone would not identify the caller.
    metadata={"outer_batch": context.batch_id, "outer_eval": context.row_idx},
)
if result.exit_code is ExitCode.TOO_FEW_REALIZATIONS:
    memo[key] = np.nan
else:
    assert result.results is not None
    assert result.results.target_objective is not None
    memo[key] = float(result.results.target_objective)
return memo[key]

np.where(MASK, INITIAL_VALUES, variables) builds the inner start point: the inner variables begin where they always do, and the outer ones carry the values being tried. The metadata tags every inner result with the outer evaluation that caused it, which is what makes the collected results traceable. The memo lookup above it is covered in Reusing an outer evaluation.

An inner optimization that ends with TOO_FEW_REALIZATIONS has no result, and the outer evaluation reports NaN for it. That is the same value an ordinary evaluation function returns for a realization that failed, so the outer optimization applies its own realization_min_success to it.

docs.title: When an inner optimization fails
docs.text:
The inner optimization is started from the outer evaluation function, so it is nested in the outer optimization. An exception it raises is raised in the outer evaluation function and aborts nothing outside the inner optimization. The evaluation function can catch it and return NaN for that realization:

try:
    result = optimize(inner_config, start, inner_function, pool=pool)
except RuntimeError:
    return numpy.nan

An exception that the outer evaluation function does not catch ends the outer optimization, as any exception from an evaluation function does. When the outer optimization is aborted, the inner optimizations are aborted with it. See Failures and Aborts for the rules that apply to every call.

docs.title: Two pools, not one
docs.text:
Each layer evaluates on its own pool, and that is a requirement rather than a preference:

# A plain dict reaches the outer evaluations because they run on threads, in
# this process; on a process pool each worker would get an empty copy.
memo: dict[tuple[float, ...], float] = {}
with session() as s:
    optimize(
        OUTER_CONFIG,
        INITIAL_VALUES,
        partial(
            inner_optimization,
            pool=s.process_pool(workers=2),
            tables=tables,
            function=partial(rosenbrock, a=a, b=b),
            memo=memo,
        ),
        pool=s.thread_pool(workers=2),
    )

The outer pool is a thread pool. Outer evaluations therefore stay inside this process, where the inner pool and the shared handler are live objects; on a process pool they would arrive as copies, which ropt refuses. The inner pool is a process pool, which is where the real work goes.

That is also where a cluster belongs. Swapping the inner pool for an hpc_pool is the whole change — the inner evaluations become cluster jobs, and the layer above is untouched:

inner_pool = s.hpc_pool(workers=50, workdir="/scratch/my-run")

Sending whole optimizations to the cluster, by putting the outer evaluations on processes or HPC, is possible but gives something different. Each outer evaluation is then copied into a job, and neither the inner pool nor the shared handler can travel with it: the job has to open its own session and collect its own results, and return them as data for you to combine. Use that when the outer evaluations are genuinely independent; use the shape above when you want one pool and one table across all of them.

Each inner evaluation is sent to the inner pool separately. Two outer evaluations can run at once, sharing the inner pool's two workers; each inner optimization's realizations compete for those workers. See How many workers.

Handing the inner optimization the pool it is already running on would deadlock, and ropt refuses it rather than hanging — see Pools inside an evaluation for why.

docs.title: Reusing an outer evaluation
docs.text:
The outer variables are integers and the outer method is population-based, so the optimizer proposes points it has already evaluated. Each repeat would run a complete inner optimization for a value that is already known. The two lines at the top of the evaluation function return the stored value instead. The memo is an ordinary dictionary, created beside the pools and passed to the function through partial.

The key is exact. Integer variables arrive as whole-numbered doubles and are re-proposed unchanged, so a repeated vector is identical bit for bit. The realization index is part of the key because a memo keyed on the variables alone gives the wrong value for a problem with more than one realization.

The dictionary is reachable only because the outer evaluations run on threads, in this process. On a process pool or an HPC pool the function is copied into a worker, which starts from an empty dictionary and discards it when it finishes, without raising. See Which pool should I use?.

Two outer evaluations run at the same time, so both can find the same key missing and both compute it. The stored value is the same either way, so the cost is one repeated evaluation. A lock would close that window and serialize the outer layer with it.

A repeat starts no inner optimization, so the table described next holds rows for the outer evaluations that were computed, not for every outer evaluation.

docs.title: Collecting results from optimizations that overlap
docs.text:
The inner optimizations are concurrent, and one handler collects them all: it takes a lock around every event it handles, so the optimizations wait for each other rather than interleaving. Give every inner optimization the same DataFrameHandler and every inner evaluation from every inner optimization lands in one table, keyed by the outer evaluation it belongs to.

Reading the answer takes one more step than usual:

best = frame.sort("Objective").row(0, named=True)
variables = [best[f"Variable,{idx}"] for idx in range(DIM)]

The outer result is not the place to look. The outer layer only ever sees its own variables and holds the inner ones at their initial values, so the optimum over all variables exists only in the collected inner results.

docs.title: Evaluating in Parallel
docs.text: Evaluations within one optimization can run in parallel, and you can run your own functions in parallel using an evaluation pool.

docs.title: Running in parallel
docs.text:
By default optimize calls the evaluation function itself, one evaluation at a time. To run the evaluations in parallel, open a session, build a pool on it and pass the pool to optimize:

from ropt import optimize, session

with session() as s:
    result = optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=s.thread_pool(workers=8))

The runnable script for this section is examples/parallel.py.

The session that created the pool releases their workers when its block ends, so most code needs no further cleanup. Nothing is implicit: an optimization evaluates its functions using the pool it was given. An optimization started with optimize without a pool has no session, and executes its function evaluations serially.

The available pools are:

  • thread_pool: runs evaluations on threads in your process.
  • process_pool: runs evaluations in reused worker processes.
  • hpc_pool: submits each evaluation as a job to an HPC cluster.

Where an evaluation runs depends on the type of pool used:

flowchart TB
    subgraph proc["your program (one process)"]
        main(["your code<br/>(main thread)"])
        seq["no pool —<br/>one eval at a time"]
        th["thread_pool —<br/>worker threads<br/>(share memory)"]
    end
    wp["process_pool —<br/>a few reused processes<br/>(data copied)"]
    clu["hpc_pool —<br/>cluster jobs<br/>(data copied)"]
    main --> seq
    main --> th
    main --> wp
    main --> clu

Threads stay inside your program and share its memory, so any Python function works and nothing is copied. The other two run the work outside it, so the objective and its data are copied there.

Only the evaluations ever leave. The optimizer itself, the pool object and your handlers all stay in the process that opened the session and started the optimization, whichever pool you choose. Throughout this page, your program means that process.

New to threads and processes?

A process is a running program with its own private memory. A thread is a worker inside a process, and all threads in a process share that memory. Threads are cheap and share data for free, but Python runs only one thread's Python code at a time. Work that waits — for a file, a network reply, an external tool — overlaps freely, because a waiting thread is not running Python code; and so does work a library performs outside Python, as numpy does while it works on an array. What is stuck one-at-a-time is arithmetic written in Python itself. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and always run truly in parallel, but they do not share memory, so data has to be copied between them, and starting one takes noticeably longer than starting a thread. A process also need not be on this machine: an HPC pool runs each evaluation as a job on a cluster, which is the same arrangement spread over more machines.

docs.title: How many workers?
docs.text:
With in a single optimization ropt parallelizes the evaluations within one optimization batch. A single optimization is a sequence of batches, and the next one cannot start before the current one is complete. Furthermore, multiple optimizations can run at the same time, each parallizing their own batches.

So the number of workers that can be kept busy is roughly

batch size  ×  optimizations running at once

capped by what the machine or the queue will actually give you. Beyond that figure the extra workers have nothing to do and sit idle.

Batch size follows from the problem, not from a setting: it is how many evaluations the optimizer requests at once. For a gradient-based optimization over an ensemble that is one per realization, plus their perturbations on the batches where a gradient is estimated. The second factor is 1 unless you run several optimizations at once, where it is the number of workers of the pool given to run.

Each evaluation in a batch is sent to a worker as a separate job. Up to workers jobs can run at once on a pool; the rest wait until a worker is available. An optimization started without a pool calls the evaluation function itself, one evaluation at a time.

You can keep several pools open at once and choose per optimization:

with session() as s:
    fast = s.thread_pool(workers=8)
    heavy = s.process_pool(workers=4)
    cheap = optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=fast)
    costly = optimize(config, x0, expensive_objective, pool=heavy)

Pools inside an evaluation

An evaluation function may start an optimization of its own, but build its pool once, in the calling code, and pass it to every evaluation. Building one per evaluation gives each a budget separate from every other: ten evaluations each building a ten-worker pool put a hundred workers on the machine, where one shared pool puts ten. Which pool it may be is a separate question, and the rules are in Pools inside an evaluation below.

Releasing a pool early

A pool holds its workers until the session that built it closes. In a loop that means opening the session inside the loop rather than around it, above all for a process pool, which holds a worker interpreter per worker:

for case in cases:
    with session() as s:
        optimize(config, case, objective, pool=s.process_pool(workers=4))

A pool used after its session has closed raises a WorkflowError rather than quietly evaluating inside your own program.

docs.title: Evaluating on threads
docs.text:
A thread_pool runs the evaluations on background threads inside your own process. Nothing is copied, so any Python function works as the objective and it can freely use the data around it:

with session() as s:
    result = optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=s.thread_pool(workers=4))

Use it when each evaluation spends most of its time waiting — starting an external program, reading a file, calling a network service. While one waits, the others run.

Threads share one Python interpreter, so arithmetic written in Python itself does not get faster on more threads. Array libraries are a different matter: numpy and its kin do their work outside Python and let the other threads run meanwhile. "My objective computes" is therefore not on its own a reason to reach past this pool — see Which pool should I use?.

docs.title: Evaluating in worker processes
docs.text:
A process_pool runs the evaluations in a handful of separate processes, reused across the optimization. Each has its own interpreter, so this is where heavy Python code actually runs faster:

with session() as s:
    result = optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=s.process_pool(workers=4))

This pool applies when the evaluation is Python code, or when each evaluation needs its own copy of something a library keeps globally. An objective that mostly runs an external program gains nothing here that a thread pool would not have given more cheaply.

The objective and its data are copied to the workers, so they must be serializable. An objective defined at module level — or in the script you ran, which each worker re-imports — works as is; a lambda, a closure, or a function defined in a notebook cell needs the cloudpickle extra (see Installation). Results can only come back through the return value; see Handlers and separate processes.

An evaluation still running when the optimization is aborted can test for it with aborting, and an external program it started with run_program is terminated, as on a thread pool. Workers still busy five seconds after the abort are killed. A program started in another way, for example with subprocess.run, keeps running after its worker is killed; see Running External Programs.

docs.title: Running on an HPC cluster
docs.text:
An hpc_pool submits each evaluation as a job to an HPC queue through pysqa; it needs the ropt[hpc] extra. workdir is required and must be an existing absolute directory on a filesystem the compute nodes share. A job is a fresh command, so the evaluation function must live in a module the job can import, which means a module installed on the compute nodes, or the ropt[cloudpickle] extra. With no further arguments it uses the default cluster and queue from the pysqa configuration of your ropt installation:

with session() as s:
    pool = s.hpc_pool(workers=10, workdir="/scratch/my-run")
    result = optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=pool)

The runnable script is examples/hpc.py. Pass it --queue local and it runs the identical optimization on the local queue, so the example works with or without a cluster.

A job is nothing more than a submission script with your evaluation command in it, and there are two mutually exclusive ways to say what that script should be: a pysqa configuration, or a template you write yourself. Both of those, and the resources a job asks for, are set out in Configuring an HPC pool at the end of this page.

docs.title: The local queue
docs.text:
The queue "local" runs each job as a process on this machine instead of on another node. It needs neither the ropt[hpc] extra nor a cluster configuration, so an objective can be tested on it before it is run on a cluster:

pool = s.hpc_pool(workers=4, queue="local", workdir="/scratch/my-run")

The cluster settings cores, memory_max, run_time_max, submit_options and query_retries are ignored, and a template or a scheduler raises a ValueError. If a cluster in the pysqa configuration defines a queue named local, queue="local" without a cluster raises an ExecutionError; pass cluster to submit to that queue.

docs.title: Which pool should I use?
docs.text:
One question rules choices out, and it is the only one you can answer by reading your own code rather than by measuring:

Does your objective read or write anything outside its arguments and its return value?

Global variables, a cache, a logger, an open file or database handle, an event handler, a counter it increments — anything at all that outlives one call.

  • No. Every pool works. Choose on speed alone, and you can swap between them freely later.
  • Yes. Stay with threads, or with no pool at all: either way the objective runs in your program, where it sees the same memory. A process or HPC pool runs the objective somewhere else, on a copy of everything it touched, so a write goes to that copy and a read sees whatever the copy was made from. No error is raised; the numbers come out wrong.

Once that is settled, the choice is about speed, and about what stopping an optimization can do:

Pool Where evaluations run Data Speeds up heavy Python? Use when none your program, one at a time shared no evaluations are fast thread_pool background threads, one process shared no — one interpreter each evaluation mostly waits (external tool, I/O), or spends its time in numpy process_pool a few reused processes copied yes each evaluation runs heavy Python code, or needs a process of its own hpc_pool jobs on a cluster copied yes each evaluation is a big cluster job How to decide, without guessing

There is no reliable rule for whether threads will scale on a given objective. "I use numpy" says almost nothing: whether the GIL is released depends on the operation, the dtype and the array size, and a real objective is a mixture whose Python-level share is invisible to the person who wrote it.

Switching to a thread pool costs one argument, and if threads do not scale on your objective the result is no speedup rather than a broken optimization. Switching to processes costs a serializable objective and a process start per worker. So try threads first:

  1. Start with a thread pool. Time workers=1 against workers=4 on a shortened optimization.
  2. If it scales, you are done, and you never needed to know what the GIL was doing.
  3. If it does not, set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (see below) and time it again.
  4. Only then move to processes.

Directional guidance is fine as orientation — waiting on an external program almost always scales, arithmetic written in Python never does, array-heavy work depends — but treat it as a place to start, and decide on the timings.

If more workers makes it slower

numpy, scipy and similar are already multi-threaded underneath, through a BLAS library that by default takes every core on the machine. Run four evaluations at once and you have four such libraries each doing that: the machine is oversubscribed several times over, the threads fight for cores, and everything slows down.

The symptom is misleading, because it reads as "parallelism does not help here" and pushes people towards processes — where the identical problem is waiting one layer down.

The fix is to give each evaluation one core's worth of library threads, before numpy is imported:

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=1

Then let the pool provide the parallelism instead.

docs.title: Pools inside an evaluation
docs.text:
An evaluation function may start an optimization of its own — that is how Nested Optimization works — and give it a pool, on two conditions.

It must be a different pool. A nested optimization waits for its own evaluations to finish, so one handed the pool it is already running on would wait for the workers it is itself occupying — a deadlock as soon as they are all busy, which is the normal case, since an optimization fills its pool with one work item per realization. Rather than hang, the pool refuses work submitted by the evaluation itself with a WorkflowError. A thread that the evaluation starts is not recognized as a worker, so work submitted from it is not refused and can still deadlock on the pool. Give the inner optimization its own pool, or none at all, so that it calls the evaluation function itself.

The evaluation must stay in your process, so on a thread pool or with no pool. On a process or HPC pool the evaluation function is copied into a worker, and a pool cannot be copied with it: open a session and build the inner pool inside the worker, or run the inner optimization without one. An evaluation function that carries a pool along anyway is refused when the work item is sent, rather than failing somewhere deep inside the optimization.

docs.title: Stopping an optimization
docs.text:
Press Ctrl-C and ropt stops dispatching new work at once. What happens to the evaluations already running depends on the pool, because what can be done to them differs:

Pool Evaluations already running none the current one finishes thread_pool aborting turns True and programs started with run_program are terminated; otherwise they run to completion process_pool as on a thread pool, and workers still busy five seconds later are killed hpc_pool the jobs are deleted from the queue; on the local queue, each job and every program it started is terminated, and killed five seconds later if still running

The optimization raises at once and does not wait for them. When the session closes, it waits up to five seconds for its pools to become idle.

A thread cannot be killed. Python provides no way to stop a running thread from outside. An evaluation on a thread pool stops early only if it checks aborting, or if the program it waits for was started with run_program. Otherwise it ends when it ends, and your program cannot exit before it does.

A process pool kills its workers after five seconds. A worker that is still busy then is killed. A program the evaluation started with run_program is terminated with it; a program started in another way keeps running.

A terminated program gets five seconds to exit. A program started with run_program, and a job on the local queue, are first asked to exit, together with every program they started. Whatever is still running five seconds later is killed.

Call restore_keyboard_interrupt in scripts that use a pool

Importing ropt changes a process-wide setting that stops Ctrl-C from breaking into a program that is waiting, and a program that waits for a thread pool or a process pool is waiting. Without the fix, Ctrl-C can have no effect at all. Call restore_keyboard_interrupt at the top of the script, after the imports; see Keyboard Interrupts.

Platforms

Outside POSIX, terminating a job on the local queue or a program started with run_program reaches only that process, and programs it started may keep running. ropt is not tested on Windows. Free-threaded (no-GIL) builds of Python are untested and unsupported.

docs.title: When an evaluation fails
docs.text:
Two kinds of failure can end an evaluation, and they reach you differently.

A failure of the machinery is one the evaluation function had no part in: a worker process is killed, a cluster job never writes its result, or the file it wrote cannot be read back. The optimization ends with an ExecutionError naming the first lost evaluation's reason. The affected evaluations do not return numpy.nan: a machine that broke is not a realization that failed to converge, and absorbing it would continue the optimization on whichever workers happened to survive and produce a result indistinguishable from one computed over the whole ensemble.

Whether the pool can run further work afterwards depends on which pool it is. An HPC pool starts fresh jobs for the next batch. A process pool kills its own workers only after an abort, which leaves no further work to run. A process pool that lost a worker in any other way, for example to the out-of-memory killer, cannot be restarted: every later batch fails the same way, and a new pool is needed.

An exception from your evaluation function is re-raised unchanged, from the optimize call, whichever pool it ran on. A bug in the objective therefore surfaces as the exception you wrote, with the pool left usable. Return float("nan") or numpy.nan instead when a realization that could not produce a value should be tolerated; see realization_min_success for how many a batch may contain before the optimization ends with TOO_FEW_REALIZATIONS.

On an HPC pool the exception crosses a process boundary, and no serialization format carries a traceback. The job therefore attaches the formatted traceback to the exception as a note, so it travels with it. An exception that cannot be serialized at all arrives as a RuntimeError carrying its repr and notes.

A job that died before writing a result leaves its only trace in the file holding its captured output. On an HPC pool that file is kept when an evaluation fails, even when the pool removes the rest, and its last lines are added to the error message. The message names the file whether or not it could be read: a shared filesystem need not show its contents yet, and a submission script that does not redirect the job's output — with #SBATCH --output={{output}} or its equivalent — never writes them at all.

docs.title: Running your own work
docs.text:
You can hand your own functions to a pool with run. It is useful when code you control — a custom handler, a custom component, or a helper you call between optimizations — has an expensive, self-contained piece of work you want to run on a pool instead of in your own code.

Pass a single callable to run it once and get its result back:

from functools import partial

from ropt import run, session

with session() as s:
    result = run(partial(expensive, data), pool=s.process_pool(workers=4))

run takes zero-argument callables — bind arguments with functools.partial or use an object method. Pass a sequence of callables to run them concurrently and get a tuple of results in order; they may be entirely different functions:

with session() as s:
    pool = s.process_pool(workers=4)
    first, second = run([partial(expensive, x), partial(other, y)], pool=pool)

As with the evaluation function on a process or HPC pool, the callables and their arguments are copied to the workers, since they run in separate processes.

On a thread pool the callables run in your process, on the pool's workers, at most workers of them at once. They are not copied, so they need not be picklable. The workers do not see the context variables of the code that called run. Without a pool, run calls the callables one after another on the calling thread, and returns when the last one has finished.

A callable given to run on a pool cannot itself call run, optimize, evaluate or evaluate_batch with that same pool: the call raises WorkflowError. Give the inner call another pool, or none.

Failures and Aborts describes how a failure or an abort reaches a run call and the calls nested in it. When a callable raises, run aborts the other callables and raises the exception at once. When an abort arrives before all of its callables have finished, run raises AbortedError. Its exit_code distinguishes an abort that was asked for from one that a failure caused, and is EXECUTOR_SHUT_DOWN when the pool could no longer run the work.

On a pool, run raises at once and does not wait for a callable that is still running. On a thread or process pool, that callable runs to its end unless it checks aborting or its program was started with run_program, and an exception it raises is logged as a warning. On a process pool its worker is killed if it is still running five seconds later. On an HPC pool it is cancelled. Without a pool, run raises when the running callable returns, and starts none of the remaining ones; it also raises if the last callable returns after the abort, since its value may come from an early return after checking aborting.

Work given to run coordinates with nothing

A callable given to run goes wherever its pool puts it, and on a process or HPC pool that is somewhere else. It may create handlers and pools of its own, but they are its handlers and its pools.

  • Results cannot be tracked across the callables. A handler created inside one sees only that callable's results and cannot be brought back: handlers cannot be moved between processes, so the return value is all that comes back. Callables that stay in your process, without a pool or on a thread pool, can feed one handler that they share, as Running Multiple Optimizations shows.
  • Worker budgets multiply, with no way around it. A pool cannot be carried into a worker process, so a callable that needs one builds its own. Four callables that each build a ten-worker pool put forty workers on the machine in four independent groups — and they do not share their effort: one with twenty pieces of work still runs ten at a time while another group sits idle. The machine carries forty workers, and never forty working on the same thing. Where evaluations stay in your process this is avoidable by sharing one pool; on a process or HPC pool it is not.

So run on a process or HPC pool fits a piece of work that is genuinely self-contained and returns its answer as a return value. When several pieces must be coordinated — counted, collected, or held to one budget — keep them in your own process instead.

Calling run from a handler holds up the optimizations feeding it

A handler runs on the thread driving the optimization, so it can call run on a pool. While it waits, it holds its own lock, so every other optimization waiting on that handler waits too.

A callable given to run that reaches back into the same handler — by starting an optimization that carries it in handlers= — fails differently per pool. On a thread pool it blocks: the handler waits for the call, and the call waits for the lock the handler holds. On a process pool it raises an ExecutionError, since a handler holds a lock and cannot be serialized. See Sharing a handler across concurrent optimizations.

An evaluation function that calls run does so without that lock held, so it does not make the other optimizations wait.

docs.title: Configuring an HPC pool
docs.text: Everything below applies only to hpc_pool. A job is a submission script with your evaluation command in it, and that script comes either from an installed pysqa configuration or from a template you write; the two cannot be combined.

docs.title: Using an installed configuration
docs.text:
This is the usual case. The configuration already describes the clusters and their queues, so all you do is pick one and say how much of it you want:

pool = s.hpc_pool(workers=10, workdir="/scratch/my-run", queue="long", cores=4)

queue names a queue defined in the configuration, which is not necessarily your scheduler's partition name — it selects a configured entry, and that entry's script determines which partition the job lands on. Ask your site which queues exist, or read them off the configuration.

When the configuration defines several clusters, cluster picks one:

  • Give cluster to select it directly; adding queue requires that queue to exist on it.
  • Give only queue and the cluster providing it is found automatically, which needs exactly one cluster to provide it — no match, or several, is an error.
  • Give neither and the configuration's own defaults apply.

config_path points at a configuration other than the installed one.

docs.title: Where the configuration lives
docs.text:
Without config_path the pool reads the site-wide configuration installed alongside ropt, at <prefix>/share/ropt/pysqa/, where <prefix> is the Python installation prefix. Deployments ship pre-configured clusters by installing them there. Find the directory with:

from sysconfig import get_paths

print(get_paths()["data"])

The directory holds a queue.yaml listing the queues, plus one submission script per queue. A minimal Slurm configuration:

queue.yaml
queue_type: SLURM
queue_primary: normal
queues:
  normal: {cores_max: 32, cores_min: 1, run_time_max: 3600, script: normal.sh}
  long:   {cores_max: 32, cores_min: 1, run_time_max: 86400, script: long.sh}
normal.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --partition=normal
#SBATCH --job-name={{job_name}}
#SBATCH --output={{output}}
#SBATCH --chdir={{working_directory}}
#SBATCH --ntasks={{cores}}
{%- if run_time_max %}
#SBATCH --time={{ [1, run_time_max // 60]|max }}
{%- endif %}
{%- if memory_max %}
#SBATCH --mem={{memory_max}}G
{%- endif %}

{{command}}

The scripts are Jinja templates, of the same form as the template described under Submitting with your own template. The partition is not among the rendered variables: it is written literally, which is why each queue normally needs its own script.

Sites with more than one cluster use a clusters.yaml naming a queue.yaml per cluster, each declaring its own queue_type; see the pysqa documentation.

docs.title: Asking for resources
docs.text:
cores, memory_max and run_time_max are passed to the submission script, and submit_options carries anything else that script declares:

pool = s.hpc_pool(
    workers=10,
    workdir="/scratch/my-run",
    queue="long",
    cores=4,
    memory_max=16,
    run_time_max=7200,
    submit_options={"account": "my-project"},
)

For account to have any effect the script must reference it. A variable a script never mentions is ignored, and one the script mentions but nobody supplies renders as empty — so a misspelling on either side drops the directive silently rather than failing. Entries that are None are dropped, so omitting a key and passing None mean the same thing. A name the pool sets itself, such as cores or queue, is rejected rather than allowed to override it.

With a configuration, resource requests are clamped to the selected queue's limits rather than rejected: asking for more cores than the queue allows quietly gets you the queue's maximum. cores is held to the queue's minimum and maximum, run_time_max to its maximum — and takes that maximum when you give no value at all — and memory_max to its maximum, but only when you pass a number. A memory string such as "4G" is passed to the submission script unchanged.

docs.title: Submitting with your own template
docs.text:
A template is the script that gets run on the cluster, written by you instead of taken from a configuration. Since there is no configuration to say what kind of cluster this is, scheduler names the queueing system to submit to — that is what determines whether it runs sbatch or bsub. It defaults to "slurm".

Nothing else is resolved for you: the queue is not an argument here, it has to be written into the script, along with everything else the scheduler needs. For Slurm that looks like this — other systems use entirely different directives:

TEMPLATE = """\
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --partition=long
#SBATCH --job-name={{job_name}}
#SBATCH --output={{output}}
#SBATCH --chdir={{working_directory}}
#SBATCH --ntasks={{cores}}
{%- if memory_max %}
#SBATCH --mem={{memory_max}}G
{%- endif %}

{{command}}
"""

pool = s.hpc_pool(
    workers=10,
    workdir="/scratch/my-run",
    template=TEMPLATE,
    scheduler="slurm",
    cores=4,
)

The script is a Jinja template, rendered by pysqa through the jinja2 package. {{name}} inserts a value and {% if name %}...{% endif %} leaves a line out when none was given, which is how the memory directive above disappears unless memory_max is set. The values available are the arguments described above — job_name, output, working_directory, cores, memory_max, run_time_max, command — plus whatever you pass in submit_options.

Two of them carry the job: {{command}} is your evaluation and the script does nothing without it, and {{output}} is the file ropt reads back to explain a failed job. A script that omits --output={{output}} still runs, but a job that dies takes the only explanation with it.

Because a template submits without a configuration, it cannot be combined with config_path, cluster or queue; passing them together raises a ValueError when the pool is created.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
hpc_pool accepts the following parameters:

Parameter Description workers Maximum number of concurrent cluster jobs (default: 1). cores Number of CPUs per job (default: 1). cluster Cluster name, when the pysqa config defines several. queue Name of a queue defined in the configuration. workdir Shared-filesystem working directory; required, and must exist. config_path The pysqa configuration directory. template A submission-script template, used instead of a configuration. scheduler The queueing system a template is written for; only meaningful with one. memory_max Memory per job. run_time_max Run time per job, typically in seconds. submit_options Extra variables for the submission script. None entries are dropped. extra_polls Extra polls to wait for a result that is missing or unreadable (default: 30).

docs.title: Running External Programs
docs.text:
An evaluation function often runs a simulator or a solver as a separate program. Start it with run_program, and the program stops when the optimization is aborted, on any pool, together with every program it started. A program started with subprocess.run or os.system keeps running after an abort, and on a thread pool the evaluation waits for it.

The example script examples/programs.py runs a simulator from the objective function. The simulator is examples/simulator.py, a stand-in for a real one: it reads the variables from a JSON input file, prints its progress, and writes the objective to a JSON output file. When the input sets hang, it sleeps for an hour instead.

docs.title: Running the simulator
docs.text:
The objective function writes the input file into a temporary directory, runs the simulator there, and reads the output file:

def objective(
    variables: NDArray[np.float64],
    context: EvaluationFunctionContext,
    *,
    hang_realization: int | None = None,
) -> float:
    """Run the simulator for one realization and read its objective.

    Args:
        variables:        The variable vector to evaluate.
        context:          Identifies the realization being evaluated.
        hang_realization: A realization whose simulator stops responding.

    Returns:
        The objective, or NaN if the simulator failed.
    """
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as workdir:
        cwd = Path(workdir)
        simulator_input = {
            "variables": variables.tolist(),
            "target": TARGETS[context.realization],
            "hang": context.realization == hang_realization,
        }
        (cwd / "input.json").write_text(json.dumps(simulator_input), encoding="utf-8")
        status = run_program(
            [sys.executable, SIMULATOR, "input.json", "output.json"],
            cwd=cwd,
            stdout="simulator.log",
            stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
        )
        if status != 0:
            return np.nan
        output = json.loads((cwd / "output.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        return float(output["objective"])

The cwd argument sets the working directory of the simulator, so the relative file names refer to the temporary directory. Each evaluation uses a directory of its own, so evaluations that run at the same time do not overwrite each other's files. The output of the simulator, standard output and standard error together, goes to simulator.log in that directory.

run_program blocks until the program exits, and returns its exit status. A status of zero usually means success; a negative status -N means that the program was ended by signal N, as in subprocess. The objective returns NaN for a failed simulation, which marks the evaluation as failed; see Failures and Aborts.

docs.title: Running the optimization
docs.text:
The optimization runs the four realizations on a thread pool, so up to four simulators run at the same time:

with session() as s:
    result = optimize(
        CONFIG, INITIAL_VALUES, objective, pool=s.thread_pool(workers=4)
    )

docs.title: Aborting a hanging simulator
docs.text:
In the second run the simulator of realization 2 does not finish. A timer calls Session.abort after two seconds:

hanging = partial(objective, hang_realization=2)
exit_code = None
start = time.monotonic()
with session() as s:
    timer = threading.Timer(TIME_LIMIT, s.abort)
    timer.start()
    try:
        optimize(CONFIG, INITIAL_VALUES, hanging, pool=s.thread_pool(workers=4))
    except AbortedError as error:
        print(f"aborted after {time.monotonic() - start:.1f} s: {error}")
        exit_code = error.exit_code
    finally:
        timer.cancel()

The abort terminates the hanging simulator, and the optimization raises AbortedError about two seconds after it started. If the objective started the simulator with subprocess.run, the abort would not reach the simulator: the session would not close until the simulator exited, an hour later. The same applies to an abort by Ctrl-C, or by an exception elsewhere in the session.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
The command is a list of the program and its arguments, as in subprocess.run. A single string raises a TypeError: there is no shell, so a string cannot be split into arguments.

Argument Description cwd The working directory of the program, by default that of your program. env The environment of the program, by default that of your program. stdout Where standard output goes. stderr Where standard error goes.

stdout and stderr take one of:

  • None, the default: the output goes where the output of your program goes.
  • A path, as a string or a Path: the file is created, or emptied if it exists, and the output is written to it. A relative path is relative to cwd.
  • An open file, or a file descriptor.
  • subprocess.DEVNULL: the output is discarded.
  • subprocess.STDOUT, for stderr only: standard error goes where standard output goes.

subprocess.PIPE raises a ValueError: to process the output, write it to a file and read the file. Standard input is empty.

docs.title: When the program is stopped
docs.text:
run_program never stops the program on its own account. It stops the program only when its caller is stopped, in one of three ways:

  • The caller is aborted, for example by Ctrl-C, by Session.abort, or by a failure elsewhere in the session. run_program then raises AbortedError; see Failures and Aborts for how that reaches the caller. Called when the caller is already being aborted, run_program raises at once and does not start the program.
  • An exception interrupts the call, for example KeyboardInterrupt in the main thread. The exception is re-raised.
  • The process that called run_program ends, for example when a process pool kills a worker that is still busy five seconds after an abort, or when an HPC job is cancelled.

In each case the program and every program it started receive SIGTERM, and those still running five seconds later receive SIGKILL.

run_program behaves the same wherever it is called: in an evaluation function, an event handler, a report callback, a function given to run, on every pool, or in your own code outside any optimization. Only the ways in which the caller can be stopped differ. Session.abort reaches code in the session's with block and the calls made there or given the session's pools. It does not reach code after the block, such as an evaluation function that you call directly, nor code in a thread that your own code starts without copying its context. In the main thread such calls still end on Ctrl-C, through the KeyboardInterrupt. In an HPC job no abort reaches the program, but cancelling the job ends the process that called run_program.

Programs that leave the process group

On POSIX the program runs in a process group of its own, and an abort signals that group. A program that it starts in a new session or process group of its own, as a daemon does, is not reached. Outside POSIX only the program itself is terminated, and programs it started may keep running.

docs.title: Restarting from the Best Point Found
docs.text:
Note

This page starts the new optimization where the previous one ended, under the same configuration. What the results at that point still cover when the configuration changes between the optimizations is described in Reusing Results at the Starting Point.

The full script for this example is examples/restart.py. It restarts the same optimization several times, each time starting from the best point the previous optimization found.

docs.title: Why restart?
docs.text: A single optimization can stop before truly converging — for example because it hit its iteration limit while still improving. Restarting runs optimize again, using the previous result as the new start point. Since each call to optimize is independent, this is a loop in your own code; ropt needs nothing special to support it.

docs.title: Seeing every evaluation
docs.text:
The best point of one optimization is all you need to start the next. To also see every evaluation across the whole sequence of restarts, pass a report callback: it is called with each FunctionResults as that evaluation finishes. A callback belongs to the optimization it is given to, so appending to one list is what carries the results across the restarts:

reported: list[FunctionResults] = []

A handler, given with handlers=, receives the same results but is an object with state of its own. One handler can be given to several optimizations, including optimizations that execute concurrently, and does more than pass results on: HistoryHandler stores every result it receives, and DataFrameHandler collects them into named DataFrames. Result Handlers covers them.

docs.title: Restart in a loop
docs.text:
Each iteration runs one optimization, starting from the previous best point, and appends its results to reported:

x0 = INITIAL_VALUES
f0: FunctionResults | None = None
g0: GradientResults | None = None
for _ in range(RESTARTS):
    result = optimize(CONFIG, x0, rosenbrock, report=reported.append, f0=f0, g0=g0)
    assert result.results is not None
    x0 = result.results.variables  # restart from the best point found so far
    f0, g0 = result.results, result.gradient

result.results.variables is the best point the optimization found — feeding it back in as x0 is the entire restart mechanism. After the loop, reported holds every evaluation from every restart, not just the last one:

print(f"evaluations collected across all restarts: {len(reported)}")
print(f"best objective after {RESTARTS} restarts: {result.results.target_objective}")

docs.title: Not evaluating the restart point again
docs.text:
The optimization that found the best point evaluated it, and returns that evaluation on result.results, together with the gradient computed at the same point on result.gradient. Passing the two back as f0 and g0 gives the next optimization those values, so it does not evaluate the point a second time.

result.gradient is None when no gradient was computed at the best point, and optimize accepts that: the perturbations at the start point are then evaluated as usual. Setting evaluation_policy to "speculative" requests a gradient at every function evaluation, which leaves a gradient available at whatever point the optimization returns.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • Restarting concurrent, rather than sequential, optimizations collects into the same handler: Result Handlers.

docs.title: Running Optimizations
docs.text:
Note

This page calls optimize and evaluate without a pool, so they evaluate one point at a time and return when they have finished. Parallel evaluation, several optimizations at once and aborting from outside need a pool from a session. Everything this page explains applies there unchanged.

Everything needed to run an optimization is imported from the ropt package itself:

from ropt import optimize

You give optimize three things:

  • a config dictionary that describes the problem — its variables, objectives, constraints and components, covered in Optimizer Setup,
  • a start point (the first set of variable values),
  • an evaluation function that returns the objective value(s) to minimize, followed by any constraint values.
import numpy as np
from ropt import optimize

config = {"variables": {"variable_count": 3, "perturbation_magnitudes": 1e-6}}

def objective(variables, context):
    return float(np.sum((variables - 1.0) ** 2))

result = optimize(config, np.zeros(3), objective)
if result.results is not None:
    print(result.results.variables)         # the best variables found
    print(result.results.target_objective)  # the objective value there

That is the basic pattern. The rest of this page explains each part and the additional options.

docs.title: The evaluation function
docs.text:
The evaluation function is a Python function with two arguments:

from ropt import EvaluationFunctionContext


def objective(variables: np.ndarray, context: EvaluationFunctionContext) -> float:
    ...
  • variables is a 1-D NumPy array: one set of variable values to evaluate.
  • context is an EvaluationFunctionContext that identifies which evaluation this is:
    • context.realization — the realization number, for a problem with an ensemble of realizations; optimize then minimizes a robust objective over all of them. See Ensemble-Based Optimization.
    • context.perturbation — the perturbation number, counted from 0, for an evaluation at a perturbed point; -1 for a function evaluation. ropt evaluates perturbed points to estimate a gradient.
    • context.function_id — the function evaluation number within the batch, counted from 0; -1 for an evaluation at a perturbed point.
    • context.batch_id — the batch number. ropt requests evaluations in batches, and each batch in a program gets its own number.
    • context.row_idx — the position of the evaluation within its batch, counted from 0.
    • context.metadata — the metadata dict the optimization was started with, if any (see Attaching metadata).

The function returns the objective value(s), followed by any constraint values. There are three ways to return them:

  • a single number when there is one objective and no nonlinear constraints;
  • a numpy vector or a sequence of numbers when there are several objectives or nonlinear constraints — put the objectives first, then the constraints;
  • an EvaluationFunctionResult when you also want to attach metadata; it holds objectives, constraints and metadata in separate fields.

If a realization fails to compute, return float("nan") or numpy.nan for it. ropt treats NaN as a failed realization and keeps going, as long as enough realizations succeed. How many is enough is set by realization_min_success, which defaults to all of them — so a single NaN ends the optimization with TOO_FEW_REALIZATIONS unless you lower it.

docs.title: Running an external program
docs.text:
When the evaluation function runs a an external program, start it with run_program. This is the supported way to run external programs from ropt. It takes the program and its arguments as a list, waits for the program to exit, and returns its exit status:

from ropt import run_program


def objective(variables, context):
    status = run_program(["my_simulator", "input.json"], cwd=workdir)
    if status != 0:
        return float("nan")
    return read_objective(workdir)

run_program terminates the program, together with every program it started, when the optimization is stopped. This matters most when evaluations run in parallel or several optimizations run at once: an abort or a failure then stops every program that is still running. A program started with the subprocess.run function from the Python standard library keeps running after an abort, so its use is not recommended. See Running External Programs.

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
optimize returns an OptimizationResult, which carries two things:

result = optimize(config, x0, objective)

result.exit_code  # why the optimization stopped (an ExitCode)
result.results    # the best evaluation, or None if none was valid

results is a FunctionResults, so the best point and its values are read from it at the paths described in Working with Results:

if result.results is not None:
    result.results.variables             # the best variables
    result.results.target_objective      # the objective value there
    result.results.functions.objectives  # the separate objective values
    result.results.functions.constraints # the nonlinear constraint values

results is None when the optimization produced no valid result: too few realizations succeeded, or no result ever satisfied the constraints — see When something goes wrong. One check therefore covers every field.

docs.title: Reporting progress
docs.text:
Pass a report callback to track the optimization as it runs. It is called once for every function evaluation, with the FunctionResults of that evaluation:

def report(result):
    print(result.variables, result.target_objective)


optimize(config, x0, objective, report=report)

To store results rather than print them, pass a handler with the handlers argument. HistoryHandler keeps every result, and DataFrameHandler collects selected fields into polars or pandas tables. See Result Handlers.

docs.title: Reporting gradients as well
docs.text:
Set report_gradients=True and the callback is also called with each GradientResults, which arrives in its own evaluation. The callback then receives both kinds and has to tell them apart:

from ropt import FunctionResults


def report(result):
    if isinstance(result, FunctionResults):
        print("objective", result.target_objective)
    else:
        print("gradient", result.target_gradient)


optimize(config, x0, objective, report=report, report_gradients=True)

Gradients are generally paired with a function evaluation at the same point. A GradientResults records an ID of that function evaluation. The uses method can be used to check if a FunctionResults object has the same ID.

docs.title: Stopping early from the callback
docs.text:
The report callback doubles as a user-defined stopping criterion: return True and the optimization stops gracefully after the current evaluation, with exit code STOPPED. Any other return value (including None) lets it continue.

from ropt import ExitCode


def report(result):
    if result.target_objective is not None and result.target_objective < 1e-6:
        return True  # good enough — stop this optimization
    return None


result = optimize(config, x0, objective, report=report)
assert result.exit_code is ExitCode.STOPPED

When running multiple optimizations at once, this stops only the optimization whose callback returned True; the others continue. To abort all running optimizations in a session, call Session.abort. For its effect when several optimizations run together, see Aborting from outside.

The runnable script is examples/stopping.py, which stops an optimization after a fixed number of results and then reads the best point it had reached.

docs.title: Attaching metadata
docs.text:
You can attach arbitrary metadata to an optimization or evaluation, from two sources:

  • Constant, per call — pass a metadata dict to optimize, evaluate, or evaluate_batch. ropt copies it onto every result the call produces, which is one way to tag an optimization:
result = optimize(config, x0, objective, metadata={"id": 7})
print(result.results.metadata["id"])   # 7

The same dict also reaches the evaluation function itself, as context.metadata — useful when the evaluation needs to know which optimization it is part of. With several optimizations at once, this is how they are told apart; see Give each optimization an ID.

  • Per evaluation — return an EvaluationFunctionResult from the evaluation function with a metadata field. This value is stored per realization, next to the objective values:
from ropt import EvaluationFunctionResult

def objective(variables, context):
    value = ...
    residual = variables - x0
    return EvaluationFunctionResult(objectives=value, metadata={"residual": residual})

result = optimize(config, x0, objective)
print(result.results.evaluations.metadata["residual"].shape)  # (3, 3)

A key does not have to be set by every realization; those that do not set it get np.nan for numeric values and None otherwise, so a numeric column with missing realizations is widened to float64 — numpy has no integer NaN. A key set by every realization keeps its natural dtype, and mixing strings and non-strings under one key raises a ValueError.

Returning an array instead of a scalar gives the key its own user-defined axis, which the names section of the configuration can label and which the DataFrameHandler spreads over one column per entry.

In the example above, the first axis is the realization; the second is the residual user-defined axis. The DataFrameHandler example shows how to label and export that axis.

Neither kind is interpreted by ropt. Constant metadata ends up on result.results.metadata; per-evaluation metadata on result.results.evaluations.metadata (one entry per realization). Both kinds can be tabulated as columns by the DataFrameHandler. See Working with Results for how each appears. The full runnable script is examples/metadata.py.

docs.title: Evaluating without optimizing
docs.text:
Sometimes you only want the objective value for a point, without running an optimizer. Use evaluate for one point and evaluate_batch for several:

from ropt import evaluate, evaluate_batch

single = evaluate(config, x, objective)
batch = evaluate_batch(config, matrix, objective)

single.results  # one FunctionResults
batch.results   # one per row of the matrix

Both return an EvaluationResult, whose results holds what the evaluation produced. What is on results is a FunctionResults, the same kind a handler receives, so everything is read the same way wherever it came from. Here result.variables is just the point you supplied.

The runnable script is examples/evaluate.py, which evaluates a single vector and then a matrix of them.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
Not every problem is an exception. An optimization that cannot make progress still returns normally, and indicates why in result.exit_code — TOO_FEW_REALIZATIONS when not enough realizations produced a value, for instance. An optimization that is aborted, for instance because another function given to the same run call raised, raises AbortedError instead (see Failures and Aborts).

Exit Codes lists all exit codes, and explains why a reason and a result are independent: result.results is None when no feasible result was ever recorded, whatever the reason the optimization ended, and an optimization that stops part-way still returns the best result it had reached before that. The evaluations it did make reach the handlers attached to it either way.

What is raised falls into three groups:

  • Mistakes in the configuration surface as a pydantic.ValidationError from the config dictionary: an unknown field, a value of the wrong type, a method name no installed plugin provides, or a set of options the chosen method does not accept. These are raised when the optimization starts, before anything is evaluated.

  • Mistakes in the call to optimize itself can raise:

    • ValueError when an argument has the wrong shape, or the evaluation function returns the wrong number of values.
    • WorkflowError when an operation conflicts with what is already happening, such as starting another optimization from inside an evaluation or reusing an object that is already in use.
    • UnsupportedError when an optional dependency is missing, or the chosen method cannot handle part of the configured problem.
    • ExecutionError when ropt cannot start or complete work needed for the optimization.
    • AbortedError when the optimization or work it started is forcefully stopped before it finishes.

  • Exceptions from your own evaluation function are not caught. They travel back from wherever the evaluation ran — including a worker thread or process — and are re-raised from the optimize call. Return float("nan") or numpy.nan instead if a failed realization should be tolerated rather than fatal.

The RoptError types above are imported from ropt itself, and catching the base class catches all of them at once:

from ropt import RoptError

It deliberately does not cover the first and third groups: configuration errors belong to pydantic, and errors from your evaluation function stay whatever you raised.

Running Multiple Optimizations shows how several optimizations can run in parallel. If a call to optimize, evaluate, evaluate_batch or run raises an exception, every call made from inside it is aborted, and the exception is raised in the code that made the call. Failures and Aborts describes each case.

docs.title: A note on enums
docs.text:
A few config values and result fields use enumerations. ExitCode, the type of result.exit_code, is imported from ropt:

from ropt import ExitCode

The enumerations that name configuration values — VariableType, BoundaryType and PerturbationType — are in ropt.enums. Their members are strings, so a configuration accepts either the member or the value it equals:

from ropt.enums import VariableType

config = {"variables": {"variable_count": 2, "types": VariableType.INTEGER}}

Writing "integer" instead gives the same configuration. A validated configuration reports these fields as enum members, whichever form was written.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Without a pool, optimize and evaluate evaluate one point at a time and return when they have finished. To access the concurrency features of ropt, open a session, build a pool with it, and pass the pool to the functions that should evaluate in parallel:

from ropt import optimize, session

with session() as s:
    pool = s.thread_pool(workers=4)
    result = optimize(config, x0, objective, pool=pool)

With a pool, optimize returns the same result, but evaluates multiple functions in parallel on the pool's workers.

docs.title: Why use a session
docs.text:
The functions without a pool are enough for a single optimization that evaluates one point at a time. A session adds the following:

  • Parallel evaluation. Pools are built by a session; see Pools.
  • Concurrent work. run, given a pool, runs optimizations, or functions of your own, on the pool's workers at the same time, and returns their results. See Running Multiple Optimizations.
  • One abort for all work. Session.abort, called from another thread, stops everything started on the session's pools or in its with block.
  • Cleanup. When the with block ends, the session stops its work and releases its workers.

Concurrency alone does not require a session: optimize calls made from threads of your own run at the same time. They are then independent: an abort or a failure in one does not reach the others. The same holds for sessions, each opened in a thread of your own, which is a way to run work that must stay independent.

Inside a session, start concurrent work with run on a pool rather than with threads of your own. An exception raised in a thread of your own stays in that thread: it does not leave the with block, so the session does not abort its other work. A function called without a pool in such a thread is not aborted with the session either. With run, the failure of one function aborts the others, and the exception is raised in your script.

docs.title: Calls without a pool in a session
docs.text: An optimization or evaluation that needs no pool calls optimize, evaluate or evaluate_batch without one in a session as well. Called in the session's with block, or from inside a call made there, they are aborted with the session. The same holds for run without a pool, which calls its functions one after another on the calling thread.

docs.title: Pools
docs.text: A pool runs evaluations in parallel, on threads, in worker processes, or as jobs on an HPC cluster. Pools are built by a session, with thread_pool, process_pool and hpc_pool, and the session releases their workers when its block ends. Several pools can be open at once. See Evaluating in Parallel.

docs.title: Failures and aborts
docs.text:
When a call to optimize, evaluate, evaluate_batch or run raises an exception, the calls made from inside it are aborted, and the exception is raised in your script. If your script does not catch it, the exception leaves the with block, and the session aborts everything that is still running. Session.abort, called from another thread, aborts every call given one of its pools or made in its with block, and the session stays aborted. Ctrl-C aborts them when the KeyboardInterrupt leaves the with block. An aborted call raises AbortedError. See Failures and Aborts and Aborting from outside.

An abort stops the programs that the aborted calls started with run_program, and every program those programs started. See Running External Programs.

docs.title: Closing the session
docs.text:
When the with block ends, the session aborts the calls that are still under way and releases its pools. It then waits up to five seconds in total for work running on its pools to end. Worker processes still busy after that are killed, and threads are no longer waited for; see Stopping an optimization.

A session cannot be opened again once it has closed. Building a pool on a closed session, or passing one of its pools to a call, raises WorkflowError.
