A session may be opened inside another, and the pools of different sessions are independent. A session opened in the with block of another, or in a call made there, is aborted with it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
A ropt optimization keeps going through a failed realization or an infeasible result, so it can end without a result to return and without raising an error. Check exit_code before using what comes back. This page collects the behaviours that most often cause confusion.

Skim it once to know what is here, then come back with a symptom and read the table of the section it belongs to.

docs.title: Results and exit codes
docs.text:
The returned result is the best feasible one. optimize returns the best result that satisfies every constraint to within constraint_tolerance, which defaults to 1e-10 and applies to bounds and linear constraints as well as nonlinear ones. If no evaluation satisfies them, the optimization ends normally with result.results set to None. The evaluations themselves are not lost: every result, feasible or not, still reaches the handlers attached to the optimization.

The return value is a summary, not the record of the optimization. It holds a single result, the best feasible evaluation. The whole history is available instead: attach a HistoryHandler or a DataFrameHandler to collect every result as it arrives. That history is also what remains when there is no best result to return.

NaN means "this realization failed", and one failure is already too many. realization_min_success defaults to all realizations, so a single NaN ends the optimization with TOO_FEW_REALIZATIONS. If some realizations are allowed to fail, set it lower:

config = {
    "variables": {"variable_count": 3, "perturbation_magnitudes": 1e-6},
    "realizations": {"weights": [1.0] * 10, "realization_min_success": 8},
}

examples/failures.py runs the same problem twice, once with the default and once allowing the failure, and prints the exit code and result of each.

Not everything that goes wrong raises. Check exit_code before using a result. The exit code gives why the optimization ended; the result is the best feasible evaluation recorded before it did, and is None only when there was none. An optimization that stops part-way therefore still returns what it had reached. See When something goes wrong.

FINISHED does not mean a limit was reached. It is the exit code for every optimization the backend ended by itself — because it converged, or because it reached max_iterations or convergence_tolerance. Those two live in the backend section and are enforced by the algorithm rather than counted by ropt, so an optimization can stop far short of max_functions, and the exit code does not distinguish which of the three applied. Only MAX_FUNCTIONS_REACHED and MAX_BATCHES_REACHED correspond to a limit ropt enforced itself.

A broken worker pool is an error, not a failed realization. When the pool itself fails — a worker process is killed, a cluster job never writes its result — the optimization stops with an ExecutionError giving the reason the first lost evaluation gave. It is not absorbed as a NaN, because a result computed over the workers that survived is indistinguishable from one computed over the whole ensemble.

What you see Most likely cause result.results is None, but exit_code is FINISHED No evaluation satisfied the constraints to within constraint_tolerance (default 1e-10; bounds and linear constraints count too), so there is no best feasible result to return. The evaluations are still in the handlers. Raise the tolerance, or check that the constraints can be satisfied at all. TOO_FEW_REALIZATIONS although only one realization failed realization_min_success defaults to all of them. Lower it. The optimization stopped long before max_functions, with FINISHED The backend ended it: max_iterations, convergence_tolerance, or its own convergence test. Those are set in the backend section; see Limiting the length of an optimization. ExecutionError part-way through an optimization The worker pool failed, not your objective. The message names the reason the first lost evaluation gave. Numbers do not match what you configured Results carry the configured values and the optimizer's scaled ones side by side; see Scaling of results.

docs.title: Your evaluation function
docs.text:
Outside your process, your objective works on a copy. On a process pool or an HPC pool, your evaluation function is sent to a worker together with the data it uses. Anything it writes there — a global, a cache, a list it appends to — is thrown away when the worker finishes. Return what you need instead; see Handlers and separate processes.

Several optimizations may call your objective at the same time. Optimizations started together with run on a pool run concurrently. Given a pool, their evaluations go there; given none, each optimization evaluates on the worker of run that runs it, so your evaluation function is called from several threads at once and has to tolerate that. See Running Multiple Optimizations.

Metadata is copied with copy.deepcopy. Every result gets its own copy of the metadata you passed, so keep it to plain data — numbers, strings, lists, arrays. A lock, an open file, or a database connection cannot be copied and raises a TypeError in the middle of the optimization.

An exception from your objective is not turned into a failed realization. It is re-raised from the optimize call, whichever pool the evaluation ran on, so a bug surfaces as the exception you wrote rather than as a missing value. Return float("nan") or numpy.nan where a realization that could not produce a value should be tolerated; see When an evaluation fails.

What you see Most likely cause A global or a cache your objective writes to is never updated The objective ran in a worker process, on a copy. Return the value as metadata instead. An objective that works alone misbehaves when several optimizations run at once It is being called from several threads at once. Remove the shared mutable state, or guard it with a lock of its own. TypeError: cannot pickle ... part-way through an optimization Something in metadata cannot be deep-copied. ExecutionError part-way through an optimization on a pool A worker or job broke, rather than your objective; see When an evaluation fails.

docs.title: Pools, stopping and processes
docs.text:
An optimization evaluates on the pool it was given, and no other. Nothing is picked up from the surrounding code. An optimization started with optimize without a pool evaluates inside your own program, on the thread that called it — even if a pool exists next to it.

Threads cannot be interrupted. Evaluations on a thread pool run to completion even after Ctrl-C, because Python cannot interrupt a thread from outside. An evaluation that checks aborting, or runs its external programs with run_program, stops early; any other evaluation that may run long and has to be interruptible belongs on a process pool or an HPC pool; see Stopping an optimization.

A process pool re-imports your script. Its workers are started with spawn, so each of them imports the file your program was started from, and everything at module level runs again in every worker. That is why the entry point has to sit behind if __name__ == "__main__":. Without the guard the workers try to start workers of their own, and building the pool raises.

A pool holds its workers until its session closes. Open the session inside the loop or function that uses it rather than around the whole program; see Releasing a pool early.

What you see Most likely cause Ctrl-C appears to do nothing A process-wide signal setting, changed by polars when ropt imports it. Call restore_keyboard_interrupt; see Keyboard Interrupts. The program will not exit after Ctrl-C Evaluations on a thread pool are still running and cannot be interrupted. Check aborting in them, or start their programs with run_program. Pages of multiprocessing tracebacks, ending in ExecutionError: Could not start worker processes The script has no if __name__ == "__main__": guard, so every worker re-ran it from the top. A process pool keeps hundreds of megabytes resident Each worker is a separate interpreter. Close the session that built the pool when the optimizations that use it are done. WorkflowError about a pool released when its session closed The pool outlived its with session() block. Build a new one inside an open session. More workers made everything slower numpy and similar libraries already use every core. Set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 and let the pool provide the parallelism; see Which pool should I use?. Simulators keep running after the optimization stopped They were not started with run_program, which terminates a program and everything it started on an abort; see Running External Programs. A cluster directive has no effect The submission script never mentions that variable, or the value was clamped to the queue's limit; see Running on an HPC cluster.

docs.title: Running many at once
docs.text:
Optimizations started together really do run at once. A handler given to all of them takes a lock around every event it handles, so it collects them safely, but a single report= callback does not: it is called by several threads at the same time. Keep such a callback free of shared state, or give each optimization its own.

A slow shared handler holds up every optimization. The optimization that emitted a result waits until the handler has finished with it, and the next one waits for the lock. Keep a shared handler cheap.

A handler must not start an optimization that reaches it again. The handler holds its own lock while it runs. A nested optimize emits on that same thread and raises; a nested optimization started with run on a pool emits on a worker of that pool, and blocks. See Result Handlers.

Not every optimizer can run beside another. A backend that needs its own working directory, writes to a fixed file name, or keeps state inside its library cannot run concurrently in one process; select it as external/... to give it a process of its own. Optimizer output capture is likewise for one optimization at a time.

What you see Most likely cause Results from a shared report= callback are jumbled or lost The callback is called from the thread of every optimization at once. Collect the results in a handler instead, or use one callback per optimization. An optimization started from a handler raises WorkflowError about the call stack, or hangs Its handler list reaches a handler that is already running; see Result Handlers. Several optimizations are slower than expected while the workers sit idle A shared handler is serializing them. Make it cheaper. A second concurrent optimization raises WorkflowError about output capture Only one optimization at a time may set stdout or stderr; see Running Multiple Optimizations.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Optimizations are reproducible by default. The seed is fixed at 1 unless you set it, so repeating an optimization reproduces its perturbations exactly. Change the seed when you deliberately want an independent repetition of the same problem.

Label tuples are checked at export, not at the start. A tuple in names that is not as long as the axis it labels lets the optimization finish normally; the mismatch surfaces later, as an error from pandas or polars when a result is turned into a table.

What you see Most likely cause RuntimeError: Auto-scaling of the objectives failed to estimate a scale factor The first batch averaged to zero, or to a value that is not finite, so no scale could be derived. Set the scales yourself, or start somewhere else. Two optimizations that should agree give different gradients Quasi-random samplers (sobol, halton, lhs) are seeded in the order the samplers are defined, so reordering that section changes the perturbations.

docs.title: Keyboard Interrupts
docs.text:
When polars is installed, importing ropt stops Ctrl-C from breaking into a program that is waiting. A program that uses a thread pool or a process pool waits for its evaluations, so there Ctrl-C can have no effect at all. Call restore_keyboard_interrupt at the top of every script that uses a pool, after the imports:

from ropt.utils import restore_keyboard_interrupt

restore_keyboard_interrupt()

docs.title: The symptom
docs.text:
You press Ctrl-C and nothing happens. Not "it takes a while" — nothing at all, however many times you press it. The optimization keeps going, and the only way out is to kill the process from another terminal.

It affects the whole program, not just the optimization: anything else that waits stops responding to Ctrl-C too.

docs.title: What causes it
docs.text:
Ctrl-C raises SIGINT, which CPython turns into a KeyboardInterrupt — but only once the interrupted thread is back in the interpreter. A thread parked in Queue.get, Event.wait, Thread.join, Future.result or Lock.acquire is not there while it waits, and whether the signal breaks that wait depends on a process-global flag called SA_RESTART.

CPython leaves the flag clear, so waits are interruptible. Some third-party extension modules install their own SIGINT handler with the flag set when they are imported. Because the flag is process-global, the effect is not confined to whoever set it: from that import onwards, Ctrl-C cannot break into any wait anywhere in the program.

This is why the symptom is hard to place. Nothing in your code changed, no error is reported, and you need not have imported the culprit yourself — a package ropt imports on your behalf is enough. Importing ropt alone sets the flag (at the time of writing by way of polars, which ropt loads whenever it is installed).

docs.title: Where to call it
docs.text: Call it after the imports, because an import is what sets the flag: calling this first and importing afterwards leaves you exactly where you started. If you import lazily, inside a function, call it after that import instead.

docs.title: Why ropt does not do this for you
docs.text:
SA_RESTART is process-global state that belongs to your program. A library that quietly changes it does so for every other part of that program, including parts that deliberately installed the handler in question — and it cannot put the flag back afterwards without restoring the very problem it was called to fix.

There is also no point at which a library could do it reliably. Any import that happens later can set the flag again, and ropt does not control when your program imports things.

So the decision is left where it can be made: in the application, by someone who knows whether the trade matters.

docs.title: What it does, exactly
docs.text:
It calls signal.siginterrupt(signal.SIGINT, True), which clears the flag and does nothing else. In particular it does not replace the SIGINT handler, so a package that chained its own keeps working; signal.signal would replace it.

It is a one-way switch on purpose. There is no context-manager form, because restoring the flag on exit would restore the hang, and a clear flag is CPython's own default in any case.

Calling it more than once is harmless, and it may be called from any thread.

Platforms

There is no SA_RESTART on Windows and therefore no problem to fix; the call is a no-op there.
